author: reek
body: MIRRORING IS OFF UNTIL IT IS TURNED ON, and the first block proves it rather than assuming it. A command is run with the flag clear and only the test's own line appears; the same shape after `serial.on` produces two more. Without the first half, a mirror that was hardwired on would pass -- and it would also mean every existing console test had started writing to the wire, which is exactly the regression this ordering catches.

author: reek
body: `serial.on` MIRRORS ITSELF, because the flag is read from the state the command produced rather than the state it was given. That is asserted here because the opposite is the more natural way to write it and fails silently in the one case anybody checks first.

author: reek
body: `serial.off` ALSO MIRRORS ITSELF, for the opposite reason: the echo is armed by the flag before the command as well as the one after it, so the last thing a far-end reader sees is the console saying it is going quiet. Without that line the stream just stops, and a mirror that was switched off is indistinguishable from a console that has hung -- the one question this module exists to answer. Both directions are asserted below, and the flag values are printed either side, because the flag flipping and the echo firing are separate failures: a `__record-set` that silently did not write left the status line reading `serial mirror ON` above a wire with nothing on it, which is how that defect was found.

author: reek
body: THE INBOUND CONVERSION IS TESTED AS TEXT, not through a port. Bytes arriving from COM1 are ASCII and Text is CCE, so `sb-append-byte` has to convert; if it did not, a remote `mem` would build a Text that is not equal to the `mem` the dispatcher matches on, and remote commands would never fire while nothing reported an error. Comparing the assembled line against a literal is what discriminates that, and it needs no serial input at all.
